title: Lost and Found: A Sheep, a Coin, and Two Sons
summary: When the Pharisees and scribes grumble that Jesus welcomes sinners and eats with them, he answers with three parables. A shepherd leaves ninety-nine sheep to find one that is lost, a woman sweeps her house to find one silver coin, and a father runs to welcome home a younger son who wasted his inheritance, then goes out to plead with the angry older son who refuses to join the celebration.
story:
Since chapter 5, Jesus' table fellowship with tax collectors and sinners has drawn complaint from religious leaders (5:29-32, 7:34, 7:39). In chapter 14 he spoke of a banquet filled with the poor and the outcast, and of a host who sends his servant into the streets. Now the objection is made directly, “This man welcomes sinners and eats with them” (verse 2), and Jesus gives his fullest answer: God is a seeker who rejoices when the lost are found, and heaven's joy is the reason for Jesus' meals.

The chapter sits near the middle of the long road to Jerusalem and at the heart of Luke's Gospel, whose summary of Jesus' mission comes a few chapters later: “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (19:10). The story of the two sons ends without saying whether the older brother goes in, leaving the grumblers of verse 2 to decide. Chapter 16 continues with parables about money addressed first to the disciples and then to Pharisees who loved money (16:14), including the rich man and Lazarus, another story about a great reversal and a father figure, Abraham, speaking to one who is outside.
historical:
Tax collectors in Galilee worked for Herod Antipas and in Judea for the Roman system, usually as agents or subcontractors who bid for the right to collect tolls and customs and profited from what they collected above the contract. They were despised as collaborators and cheats (3:12-13, 19:8). ‘Sinners’ covered those whose way of life openly broke the Law or who worked in dishonored trades. Sharing a table meant accepting someone, and the Pharisees, who cared about purity and tithing at meals, avoided eating with people who did not keep those rules. How far the Pharisees extended priestly purity into ordinary life is debated. E. P. Sanders (Jesus and Judaism, 1985) argued that ‘sinners’ here means the wicked, those who flagrantly and persistently broke the Law, and that the offense lay in Jesus welcoming them without first requiring the recognized signs of repentance, such as restitution and sacrifice. James D. G. Dunn (Jesus, Paul and the Law, 1990) replied that ‘sinners’ was also a factional label that one Jewish group used of others whose observance it judged inadequate. On any reading, the complaint in verse 2 is an accusation that Jesus has compromised himself by the company he keeps.

Inheritance law stands behind the third story. The firstborn received a double share (Deuteronomy 21:17), so with two sons the younger's portion was a third. A father could make a gift of property during his lifetime while keeping its use and produce until death, and the Mishnah prescribes the formula ‘from today and after my death’ for such gifts (m. Bava Batra 8:7). The wisdom book of Sirach, from the early second century BC, warns a father never to give his property to a son while he lives, lest he regret it and have to ask for it back (Sirach 33:20-24). The father in the parable divides his property between both sons (verse 12), which is why he can tell the older son that all he has is his (verse 31).

The far country is Gentile land, as the pigs show. The Law counts pigs unclean (Leviticus 11:7, Deuteronomy 14:8), and the Mishnah forbids Jews to raise them anywhere (m. Bava Kamma 7:7). Carob pods (keratia) were fodder for animals and food for the destitute; a saying attributed to Rabbi Aha in Leviticus Rabbah 13:4 holds that when Israel is reduced to eating carob pods, they repent. Famines were a real part of ancient life, and Acts records one in the reign of Claudius (Acts 11:28).

The lost sheep has a parallel in Matthew 18:12-14, where it addresses the disciples' care for little ones who stray and ends with the Father's will that none should perish. The Gospel of Thomas, saying 107, has a version in which the lost sheep is the largest of the flock and the shepherd loves it more than the ninety-nine. The lost coin and the two sons appear only in Luke. Kenneth Bailey, who taught the New Testament for four decades in Egypt, Lebanon, Jerusalem, and Cyprus, studied these parables in the light of Middle Eastern village life (The Cross and the Prodigal, 1973; Poet and Peasant, 1976; Finding the Lost, 1992), and much popular teaching on Luke 15 depends on his work. How far modern village custom can illuminate first-century Galilee is disputed, as the interpretation section below explains.
cultural:
A hundred sheep was a modest flock, often held by a family or shared among several; leaving the ninety-nine in the open country assumes others were watching them. A lost sheep tends to lie down and refuse to move, which is why the shepherd carries it home across his shoulders, the posture of the early Christian images of the Good Shepherd. The shepherd was a familiar figure for Israel's kings and for God himself (Psalm 23, Isaiah 40:11, Ezekiel 34), yet ordinary shepherds were often counted among the trades of low repute in later rabbinic lists. Jesus asks his critics to imagine themselves in that role: ‘What man among you’.

The ten silver coins were drachmas, Greek coins roughly equal in value to the Roman denarius, a laborer's day wage (Matthew 20:2). For a poor household ten of them could be a large part of its savings; Joachim Jeremias suggested they might have been a dowry worn on a headdress, which the text does not say. Village houses had small windows or none and floors of beaten earth or rough stone, so she lights a lamp and sweeps, listening and looking for the coin. Her women friends and neighbors (the Greek forms are feminine) are called to share her joy. Setting a woman's search beside a man's is a habit of Luke's (compare 13:18-21).

In the third story, a younger son's request for his share while his father was alive was unusual, and selling it off quickly (verse 13, ‘gathered everything together’) turned family land into cash. Kenneth Bailey argued that in village culture the request amounted to wishing the father dead, that the father would be expected to refuse and punish it, that an elderly landowner running in public, hitching up his robe, was a shameful act, and that the father ran to reach his son before the village could publicly cut him off. Critics reply that no ancient source shows the request meant wishing the father dead, that lifetime division of property is attested (m. Bava Batra 8:7), and that the evidence for village ceremonies of rejection is late. Feeding pigs for a Gentile in a foreign land and envying their food was the lowest point imaginable for a Jewish son. His rehearsed confession echoes Pharaoh's words to Moses, ‘I have sinned against the LORD your God and against you’ (Exodus 10:16), a parallel that some take as a sign the speech is calculated and others as simply the biblical form of confession.

The father's gifts restore status. When Pharaoh raised Joseph over Egypt, he gave him his signet ring and fine linen robes (Genesis 41:42), and the returning son receives the best robe and a ring. Sandals marked a free member of the household; slaves and the very poor often went barefoot. The fattened calf was kept for a great occasion, and it provided more meat than one family could eat, so the feast would include the village. Music and dancing (sumphōnia and choroi, verse 25) were the sounds of weddings and great celebrations (Jeremiah 31:13). The older son's complaint that he never received even a young goat to celebrate with his friends measures the difference: a goat for a few friends, a calf for a whole village. His words about prostitutes (verse 30) are his own accusation; the narrator said only that the younger son lived wastefully (verse 13).
literary:
The three parables form one answer: verse 3 calls it ‘this parable’, singular. Each follows the same pattern: something lost, a search or a waiting, something found, and a celebration with others. The numbers narrow from one in a hundred to one in ten to one of two, and the value rises from livestock to money to a son. The first two stories are introduced with questions that draw the hearers in (‘What man among you’, ‘what woman’) and end with explicit statements about joy in heaven (verses 7 and 10). The third is longer, begins with a statement rather than a question, and has a second act.

The story of the two sons is built with care. The younger son's decline has three stages (he spends everything, famine strikes, he feeds pigs) and his recovery begins with an inner speech, a device Luke uses in several parables (12:17-19, 16:3-4, 18:4-5). The speech he rehearses (18-19) is cut short when he delivers it (21); the father never lets him reach the request to be made a hired servant. The father's actions come in a rush of verbs, he saw, was filled with compassion, ran, embraced, kissed (verse 20), and the son's words are answered not with words to him but with orders to the servants (22-23). The refrain ‘was dead and is alive again; was lost and is found’ closes both acts (verses 24 and 32).

The second act mirrors the first. The father went out to the younger son; now he goes out to the older (verse 28). The younger son addressed him as ‘Father’; the older begins with ‘Look’ and describes his years at home as slaving (douleuō, verse 29). He calls his brother ‘this son of yours’ (verse 30); the father answers with ‘this brother of yours’ (verse 32) and calls him teknon, ‘child’ (verse 31), a warmer word than son. The story ends open, with the father pleading and the older son outside, mirroring the Pharisees and scribes outside the celebration of verses 1 and 2. The reader is left where Jesus' first hearers were, deciding whether to go in. Many interpreters have noted that the pattern of two brothers, in which the younger is favored, runs through Genesis (Cain and Abel, Ishmael and Isaac, Esau and Jacob, Joseph and his brothers), and Kenneth Bailey argued in Jacob and the Prodigal that Jesus retells Jacob's story in this parable.

outline.t: Sinners gather, and the religious grumble
The younger son leaves and loses everything
The son returns and the father runs
The older son outside the feast

doctrines.note: The first two stories end with joy over ‘one sinner who repents’ (verses 7 and 10), though a sheep and a coin do nothing but get found: repentance is the human side of being found by God. The younger son shows what it looks like from the inside, coming to his senses and returning with confession (verses 17-21), and the father's welcome runs ahead of it.

Jesus pictures God through a shepherd, a woman sweeping her house, and a father, and the same character shows in each: God seeks, searches until he finds, and rejoices with others. The father goes out to both sons, the rebellious and the resentful, and heaven's joy, not grudging tolerance, is God's response to the returning sinner.

In each story the initiative is the owner's: the shepherd goes after the sheep, the woman sweeps, the father sees and runs. Restoration comes as a gift before the son can bargain for it: robe, ring, sandals, and feast answer the request he never finished making (verses 21-24). Salvation is being found and brought home, from death to life.

The older son counts his standing by years of service and commands kept (verse 29), which is why his father's generosity to his brother feels like injustice. The parable does not deny his obedience, but it shows that obedience reckoned as wages cannot share the father's joy. Paul's contrast between a gift and wages (Romans 4:4-5) names the same difference.

The father's love is moved before any confession (verse 20) and is just as patient with the older son, to whom he says, “Son, you are always with me”, and adds, “all that is mine is yours” (verse 31). Love in the parable is shown by going out, embracing, restoring, and pleading, and it calls the older son to love his brother in turn.

words.note: Apollumi, to lose, destroy, and in the middle voice to be lost or perish. It occurs about 91 times in the New Testament, 27 of them in Luke, and eight times in this chapter: the sheep, the coin, and the son are lost, and the son is perishing with hunger (verse 17). Its range covers both being missing and being ruined. In Luke, being lost is not only moral failure but danger, and the word invites rescue rather than contempt. Luke's summary of Jesus' mission uses the same participle: to seek and save the lost (19:10).

Heuriskō, to find, discover. It occurs about 176 times in the New Testament, 45 of them in Luke, and eight times in this chapter, always answering lost: until he finds it, rejoice with me for I have found, he was lost and is found. The aorist passive in verses 24 and 32, heurethē, ‘he was found’, leaves the finder unnamed, in the reverent style that often implies God as the actor.

Diagonguzō, to grumble, murmur among themselves. It occurs only twice in the New Testament, both in Luke: here (verse 2) and at Zacchaeus's house (19:7), where the same complaint about Jesus eating with a sinner recurs. The Greek Old Testament uses it for Israel murmuring against God and Moses in the wilderness (Exodus 16:2, 16:7; Numbers 14:2). The Pharisees' complaint puts them, like the older brother, among those who resent God's generosity.

Prosdechomai, to receive, welcome, and also to wait for. It occurs about 14 times in the New Testament, five in Luke, who uses it of Simeon and Anna waiting for the consolation and redemption of Israel (2:25, 2:38) and of Joseph of Arimathea waiting for the kingdom (23:51). In verse 2 it is the critics' word for what Jesus does with sinners: he ‘welcomes’ them. Paul uses it for the church's welcome of one another (Romans 16:2, Philippians 2:29).

Splagchnizomai, to be moved with compassion, from splagchna, the inner organs where ancient people located deep feeling. It occurs 12 times in the New Testament, all in the Synoptic Gospels, three of them in Luke: of Jesus at Nain (7:13), of the Samaritan (10:33), and of the father here (verse 20). In each case it moves someone to act for a person in desperate need. The father feels it while the son is still far off, before any confession.

Chara, joy. It occurs about 59 times in the New Testament, eight of them in Luke. The angels announce good news of great joy at Jesus' birth (2:10), and here Jesus speaks of joy in heaven over one sinner who repents (verses 7 and 10). The related verbs chairō and sugchairō, to rejoice and to rejoice with, run through verses 5-9. In the third story the joy becomes a feast, and the question is who will share it.

Euphrainō, to make glad, and in the middle or passive to celebrate, make merry. It occurs about 14 times in the New Testament, six in Luke, four of them in this chapter (verses 23, 24, 29, 32). Luke also uses it of the rich fool who tells himself to be merry (12:19) and the rich man who feasted every day (16:19), a contrast with the father's celebration, which is shared and has a reason. In verse 32 the father says it ‘was necessary’ (edei) to celebrate.

Asōtōs, wastefully, recklessly, prodigally. This adverb occurs only here in the New Testament (verse 13). The related noun asōtia describes debauchery in Ephesians 5:18, Titus 1:6, and 1 Peter 4:4. Its root sense is being beyond saving, spendthrift, and the adverb itself says wasteful rather than naming a specific immorality; the charge of prostitutes comes from the older brother (verse 30). The English name ‘prodigal’, meaning wasteful, comes from the Latin tradition's description of the son.

christ:
These parables are Jesus' defense of his own practice of welcoming sinners and eating with them. By telling them, he claims that in his meals with tax collectors God himself is doing what the shepherd, the woman, and the father do: seeking, finding, and rejoicing over the lost. The Old Testament had promised that God would search for his scattered sheep himself after Israel's shepherds had failed to seek the lost (Ezekiel 34:4, 34:11-16), and the Greek of Ezekiel 34:16 uses the same participle for ‘the lost’ as Luke. Jesus acts as that shepherd, and his word in 19:10 makes the claim explicit.

The parables do not say in so many words that Jesus is the shepherd or the woman or the father, and Christian readers have handled that reticence in different ways. Gregory the Great (Homilies on the Gospels 34) read both the shepherd and the woman as Christ, God and the Wisdom of God, and the woman's lamp as the divinity shining in the earthen vessel of his flesh. Others read the father as God the Father and Jesus as the one who tells the story and embodies the father's welcome at his table. Either way, the chapter shows the heart of God that Jesus reveals and enacts: he is accused of welcoming sinners, and the accusation is true.

The younger son's return has been read as a picture of the gospel's movement from death to life (verses 24 and 32), language Paul uses of those made alive together with Christ (Ephesians 2:1-5). The older son's refusal shows that the danger of being lost belongs to the religious as much as to the reckless, and the father's pleading with him anticipates Jesus' grief over Jerusalem (13:34, 19:41). The one who tells this story will himself be counted among sinners (22:37), will promise paradise to a dying criminal (23:43), and after his resurrection will send his disciples to preach repentance and forgiveness in his name to all nations (24:46-47). The feast the father throws is a foretaste of the table Jesus promises in his kingdom (22:29-30), and the open ending invites every older brother, including every religious reader, to come in.
interpretation:
The church fathers read the two sons in two main ways. Augustine (Questions on the Gospels 2.33) and Jerome, answering Pope Damasus in Letter 21 (383), took the older son as Israel and the younger as the Gentiles, though Jerome also allowed a reading of the righteous and the sinner. Tertullian, writing as a Montanist in On Modesty (chapters 7 to 9), rejected any use of the parable to restore Christians who had committed grave sin after baptism: the lost sheep, the coin, and the prodigal, he argued, were pagans coming to faith, and parables must not be pressed for every detail. Ambrose treated the parables at length in book 7 of his Exposition of Luke, and Peter Chrysologus, bishop of Ravenna in the fifth century, preached a series of sermons on the prodigal son. Gregory the Great (Homilies on the Gospels 34) read the ninety-nine as the angels, and the woman's ten coins as the nine orders of angels with humanity as the tenth, created so that the number of the elect might be complete.

The Reformation and modern Protestantism made the third parable a touchstone. In the nineteenth century many liberal theologians called it the gospel within the gospel, the whole message of God's fatherly love without need of atonement; B. B. Warfield answered in a sermon on the parable (published in The Saviour of the World, 1913) that the parable teaches much but not the whole gospel, and that the heart of the gospel, the cross, is not in it. Adolf Jülicher's work on the parables (1888 to 1899) insisted that each parable makes a single point, C. H. Dodd and Joachim Jeremias (The Parables of Jesus, German 1947) set Luke 15 in the conflict over Jesus' table fellowship, and Jeremias stressed that the story's weight falls on the older son as well as the younger. Helmut Thielicke's sermons (The Waiting Father, English 1959) and Timothy Keller's The Prodigal God (2008) popularized the view that the parable exposes both irreligious and religious lostness.

Kenneth Bailey's cultural readings (The Cross and the Prodigal, 1973; Poet and Peasant, 1976; Finding the Lost, 1992; Jesus Through Middle Eastern Eyes, 2008) shaped a generation of preaching: the request as a death wish, the father's running as self-humiliation, and the father's public costly love as a picture of the cross. His critics include Klyne Snodgrass (Stories with Intent, 2008), who warned that Bailey assumed too much continuity between modern villagers and first-century Galileans and read the parable for what is not in it, and Amy-Jill Levine (Short Stories by Jesus, 2014), who argued that such readings rest on late or modern evidence and often portray Jewish culture as harsh so that Jesus can look gracious. Levine reads the story as about a man who had two sons and nearly lost count of one, and she stresses the father's words to the older son. Mark Allan Powell (What Do They Hear?, 2007) found that American readers retelling the story rarely mentioned the famine, while most Russian readers in St. Petersburg did, a reminder that every culture hears its own details.

The parable is among the most painted and staged in Christian art. Albrecht Dürer's engraving The Prodigal Son amid the Swine (about 1496) shows the son kneeling among pigs; Rembrandt made an etching of the return in 1636 and, near the end of his life, the great painting The Return of the Prodigal Son (late 1660s, now in the Hermitage, Saint Petersburg). Henri Nouwen's The Return of the Prodigal Son (1992), written after he sat before the painting in 1986, reads it as a call to recognize oneself in both sons and finally to become the father. In music there are Arthur Sullivan's oratorio The Prodigal Son (1869), Prokofiev's ballet for George Balanchine and the Ballets Russes (1929), and Benjamin Britten's church parable The Prodigal Son (1968); in literature, André Gide's The Return of the Prodigal Son (1907). In Lutheran Leipzig Luke 15:1-10 was the Gospel for the Third Sunday after Trinity, and Bach's cantatas Ich hatte viel Bekümmernis (BWV 21) and Ach Herr, mich armen Sünder (BWV 135) belong to that day. The Orthodox churches keep the Sunday of the Prodigal Son as the second Sunday of the Triodion before Great Lent. In the Revised Common Lectionary, Year C, 15:1-3 and 11b-32 are read on the Fourth Sunday in Lent and 15:1-10 in September (Proper 19); the Roman lectionary reads 15:1-3 and 11-32 on the Fourth Sunday of Lent and the whole chapter on the Twenty-fourth Sunday in Ordinary Time in Year C.
text:
Two differences between manuscripts affect what English Bibles print. In verse 21 Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus, Codex Bezae, and a few others let the son finish his rehearsed speech by adding ‘make me like one of your hired servants’. Most editors, including the committee behind the United Bible Societies' text as Bruce Metzger explains, judge the words to be a scribal harmonization with verse 19, since copyists tended to make repeated speeches match, and the King James Version and most modern versions omit them; some modern versions mention them in a note. Without them the story makes its point by the interruption: the father will not hear his son propose to become a servant.

In verse 16 the earliest manuscripts, including P75, Sinaiticus, and Vaticanus, read that he longed ‘to be fed with’ (chortasthēnai ek) the pods, while Codex Alexandrinus and the later Byzantine manuscripts read ‘to fill his belly with’ (gemisai tēn koilian autou apo), the blunter wording the King James Version follows and the BSB also reflects. In verse 22 the earliest manuscripts include tachu, ‘quickly’, at the head of the father's orders, which later copies omit. None of these changes the meaning of the story.

teach.big: God seeks the lost and rejoices when they are found, and the question the chapter leaves with every listener, the reckless and the respectable alike, is whether they will come in to share his joy.

outline.t: Jesus welcomes sinners, and the complaint of the religious sets the question the whole chapter answers.
God goes after the one who is lost and carries it home rejoicing; heaven's joy over one repentant sinner outweighs the self-assured.
God searches diligently, like a woman sweeping her house for one coin, and joy is meant to be shared with others.
Sin is first a departure from the Father, and it ends in emptiness and hunger in a far country.
Repentance comes to its senses and goes home; the Father runs, embraces, and restores sonship before the confession is finished.
The Father goes out to the resentful religious son too; obedience reckoned as wages cannot share his joy, and the invitation stands open.

teach.pitfalls:
The most common misuse preaches the parable of the two sons as if it ended at verse 24, a story about the younger son's repentance, and leaves out the older son, to whom the parable was actually addressed (verses 2-3). A second makes the parable a complete theology of salvation that needs no cross; parables make a few points and do not say everything (see the hard question below). A third fills the story with cultural claims the text does not make, such as the father's shame in running or a village ceremony of rejection, and preaches them as fact; if used, they should be offered as one scholar's reading that others dispute.

Avoid turning the older son into a caricature of Jews or of Pharisees in general. Jesus addresses real critics, but the father affirms the older son's place (verse 31) and pleads with him, and the ending is open. Avoid using the lost coin and sheep to suggest that repentance is unnecessary because God does everything, and avoid the opposite error of making the younger son's rehearsed speech a model prayer that earns his welcome; he is embraced before he says it. Finally, do not let the familiar title ‘prodigal son’ hide the father, who is the story's central figure from first line to last.
teach.pastoral: Parents whose children have walked away from faith or from the family will hear this chapter personally, often with grief and guilt. Be careful not to promise that every prodigal will return, and do not imply that a child's leaving proves parental failure; the father in the story did nothing wrong. Let them see a father who watches the road and runs. Those who feel like the older son, faithful for years and unthanked, need to hear the father's tender words (verse 31) before they are challenged. People carrying shame for a wasted past, addiction, or sexual sin will hear the younger son's story; stress the embrace before the confession. And for those whose earthly fathers were absent or cruel, the picture of God as father may be hard: the shepherd and the woman sweeping her house show the same seeking love in other forms.

hard.q: The father forgives without any sacrifice or payment. Does the parable of the two sons make the cross unnecessary?
hard.a:
The objection has been pressed from several directions. Faustus Socinus, in De Jesu Christo Servatore (published 1594), argued that God, like a creditor, can freely remit a debt without satisfaction, and many liberal Protestant readers of the nineteenth century called this parable the gospel within the gospel, finding in it the whole of Jesus' message: God is a Father who forgives the repentant, and later doctrines of atonement add what Jesus did not teach. Jewish readers have made a related point with force: the parable teaches what Judaism has always taught, that God receives the one who returns. The prophets call Israel to return with the promise of mercy (Hosea 14:1-4, Ezekiel 18:21-23), and the Mishnah teaches that repentance, with the Day of Atonement, atones for sin (m. Yoma 8:8). On this view the parable needs no mediator at all.

Christian responses begin with genre. A parable makes one or a few points, and this one answers the grumbling of verse 2 by showing God's joy over a returning sinner; it says nothing about how God's forgiveness is made possible, just as it says nothing about the Spirit or the resurrection. B. B. Warfield made this argument in a sermon on the parable (The Saviour of the World, 1913): the parable teaches the Father's welcome, but the heart of the gospel is not in it. Luke's Gospel as a whole speaks plainly about the cost. The Son of Man must suffer (9:22), his blood is poured out for his disciples in a new covenant (22:20), and the risen Christ says repentance and forgiveness are preached in his name because he suffered (24:46-47). Some interpreters, including Kenneth Bailey (The Cross and the Prodigal, 1973), also find cost within the story itself: the father bears loss, public exposure, and the pain of rejection in order to restore both sons, a picture of costly love that points toward the cross, though critics doubt some of the cultural evidence behind that reading. Many readers add that the one telling the story is himself the Father's welcome made flesh, and that his meals with sinners (verse 2) are where the parable's forgiveness is being offered. On the Jewish objection, Christians can gladly agree that God receives the returning sinner, as the prophets said; the Christian claim is that Jesus is the one in whom that return and that welcome now take place.

hard.q: Is the older brother a portrait of the Jewish people, or of Pharisees in general?
hard.a:
The reading that makes him so is old and was once standard. Augustine (Questions on the Gospels 2.33) and Jerome (Letter 21) identified the older son with Israel and the younger with the Gentiles, and generations of preaching treated the older brother as the type of Jewish legalism, jealous of grace to outsiders. Jewish readers, among them Amy-Jill Levine (Short Stories by Jesus, 2014), have pointed out how this reading feeds contempt for Judaism: it takes a story Jesus told to fellow Jews, in which a Jewish father loves both sons, and turns one of them into a caricature of a whole people. Levine argues that the parable is about a family, that the older son's complaint is understandable, and that the father's last words affirm him.

The responses start from the text. Luke says Jesus told the parables to the grumbling Pharisees and scribes (verses 2-3), so the older son does mirror their complaint; but Jesus' hearers on every side were Jews, including the tax collectors and sinners, and the younger son in the story is as Jewish as the older. Tertullian (On Modesty 8-9) already objected that the Israel-and-Gentiles reading does not fit the details, since the older son never leaves the father's house and is told that all the father has is his. The father does not reject the older son. He goes out to him as he went out to the younger, calls him teknon, ‘child’, assures him of his place (verse 31), and pleads with him to come in, and the story ends before he answers. Most modern commentators, Christian and Jewish, read the older brother as a warning to religious people of every kind, including Christians, who resent God's mercy to those they consider less deserving. Whether Luke's own framing (verses 1-2) sharpens the parable against the Pharisees more than Jesus did is debated; what the story itself leaves is an open door and a pleading father.

observe: What complaint do the Pharisees and scribes make in verse 2, and to whom does Jesus tell the parables?
What four things does the pattern of each story contain (something lost, a search, a finding, a celebration)? Trace them in all three.
Compare the younger son's rehearsed speech (verses 18-19) with what he actually says (verse 21). What is missing, and why?
interpret: Why do you think the third parable ends without telling us whether the older son went in?
The older son says ‘this son of yours’ and the father answers ‘this brother of yours’. What does that exchange reveal about each of them?
What does the chapter teach about repentance, given that a sheep and a coin cannot repent, yet Jesus speaks of joy over ‘one sinner who repents’?
apply: Which character do you most identify with: the younger son, the older son, or the father? Which do you most need to become?
The older brother was faithful, yet he stayed outside the celebration. Why can religious faithfulness make it harder to rejoice over God's grace to others?
The shepherd, the woman, and the father all go to great lengths to find what was lost. What would it look like for your church to share that kind of search?
